ordered_diagnoses: Primary cutaneous CD4-positive small/medium T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder

facts.raw_span: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face
slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of erythroderma, confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques, and epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes is consistent with mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

The patient's widespread erythroderma, bilateral lower-lid ectropion, and lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis are features that can be seen in Sézary syndrome, an aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

The patient's presentation of erythroderma, atypical lymphocytes, and immunohistochemical staining positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7 is consistent with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a rare and aggressive type of blood cancer.

The patient's presentation of erythroderma, atypical lymphocytes, and CD30 positivity in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes is consistent with cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma, a group of rare and heterogeneous lymphomas.
